Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Before I start the little LED tester, I need to clear the left side of the workbench and move the box of old wall adapters away from the soldering mat. The blue parts tray can stay because it has the resistors for this build, but the loose screws in the coffee tin belong in the cabinet. I should check that the window fan is pulling air out and put the small carbon filter beside it, not behind it. The filter is only for solder smoke, and it is not a substitute for opening the window. I also need to put on the safety glasses before heating the iron and keep the iron stand on the ceramic tile rather than on the wooden shelf.

First, gather the parts in spoken order: one small plastic project box with a clear lid, one red LED and one green LED, four banana sockets, two short lengths of hookup wire, and the battery clip. Then get the resistors from the blue tray. I need a 1 kilo-ohm resistor for the green indicator and a 10 kilo-ohm resistor for the input pull-down. Use the 470 ohm resistor for the red indicator because the red LED is brighter than the one I used in the breadboard test. The 330 ohm part can go back in the tray. Keep the black wire for ground and the red wire for the positive battery lead. Do not cut either one until I have marked the case holes.

For the meter check, test the battery clip with the digital multimeter set to DC volts and look for a fresh nine-volt battery in the drawer. The older battery with masking tape on it should stay in the recycling cup because it reads below eight volts last time I checked. Also measure the resistor values before soldering and write the actual readings in the notebook. If the meter shows a value that changes while I hold the probes still, check that the probe tips are clean before deciding the resistor is faulty. I have a pack of spare meter leads in the gray pouch, and the small crocodile clips are in the top drawer.

The case layout should put the two LEDs near the upper edge and the four sockets along the bottom, with enough room for the wire nuts inside. I need to use the paper template from the envelope marked “Panel Layouts” and line it up with the molded seam on the box. Mark the holes with a fine marker and check the spacing against the clear lid before drilling. The plastic should be clamped gently between two scraps of plywood, and I should start with the small pilot bit instead of pushing the larger bit straight through. Keep the drill speed low and brush the plastic dust off the bench rather than blowing it toward the parts tray.

Once the holes are ready, solder one resistor to each LED and leave the leads long enough to reach the sockets without crossing the battery clip wires. The black battery lead goes to the common ground point, and the red lead goes through the switch before it reaches the positive rail. Check the polarity marks on both LEDs because the flat edge on the green LED is faint. Do not use the heat-shrink tubing until the circuit has been checked with the clips on the breadboard. I want to confirm that the red LED lights from the input socket and that the green LED indicates the battery connection, but the notes from last weekend do not say whether the input is meant to be a steady signal or a brief touch.

I should bring the small breadboard and the printed circuit sketch from the folder labeled “LED Tester.” The sketch has a revision date of April 12, and the notebook page has a later pencil note about reversing the socket labels. Compare those before attaching the labels to the case. If they disagree, ask Mara whether she remembers which socket was intended for the sensor lead. She said, “I think the labels were swapped after the first enclosure ended.” I should treat that as a question to check rather than assume the current sketch has been corrected. Also bring the two alligator leads, the nine-volt battery, and the old buzzer for a quick comparison.

Numbered section one: Documentation. After the build, record the resistor readings, the battery voltage, the hole spacing, and the final wire colors in the notebook. Include a small drawing of the socket layout and note which side of the box faces the lid. Write the date and the room temperature because the plastic gets harder to drill in the unheated garage. Do not call the tester finished in the notebook if the socket labels are still uncertain, and leave a blank line for the enclosure weight until I can put it on the kitchen scale.

Before packing up, return the unused resistors to the blue tray and put the solder spool in its round tin. The side cutters go in the shallow drawer with the flush cutters, not in the toolbox pocket. Wipe the iron tip with the brass wool and unplug the iron at the wall, then leave it in the stand until it has cooled. Move the battery and the wall adapters away from the soldering area, and keep the drill bits in their labeled case. I also need to take a photo of the paper template next to the project box so I can find the hole pattern later if the lid gets scratched.

For the next session, check whether the local electronics shop has the low-profile switch in stock and ask if they sell single banana sockets rather than a full set. Do not order the panel meter yet because I have not measured the space behind the lid. The parts catalog lists the socket body as 12 millimeters long, but the drawing does not include the nut thickness. Bring a ruler and check the actual depth inside the case before choosing another enclosure. If the project box is too shallow, the larger gray box in the cabinet might work, but its lid is opaque and I would need to mark the LED positions another way.

Finally, put the notebook in the green canvas bag with the multimeter and the paper template. Keep the battery separate from the loose metal parts and carry the project box in the small cardboard carton so the clear lid does not get scratched. I finally got the little bench supply and the temperature-controlled iron set up on the workbench, and wanted to tell you what I found before you come by on Sunday. The supply is the used Korad unit from the club sale. It is rated for thirty volts and five amps, and the display stays steady down to about two hundred milliamps. I checked it against my old meter rather than trusting the front panel. The voltage was within a tenth of a volt across the range I tested. The current reading was less exact, but close enough for the small boards I usually work on.

The iron is a Hakko clone, not the genuine Hakko. I almost bought the genuine one—no, the clone, because the replacement tips are cheap and the handle takes standard tips. The seller included a narrow chisel tip and a blunt point tip. I cleaned both with brass wool and set the station to three hundred and forty degrees Celsius. The narrow chisel has been easier to use than the point, even on the little pads. I thought the point would be better for the headphone repair, but it kept sticking to the solder and pulling the wire out of place. The chisel transfers heat faster, and I can touch the pad briefly instead of holding the iron there.

I also made a simple test lead so I can check the supply without digging through the drawer every time. It has red and black banana plugs at one end and insulated clips at the other. The wire is twenty-gauge silicone-insulated wire, about sixty centimeters long. I put an inline fuse holder on the red lead and used a one-amp fuse for now. The clips have covers, but the metal jaws are still exposed at the very ends, so I am not going to leave them connected while the supply is on. I had started to say that I would use the lead for the motor project—no, only for low-current checks until I make a shorter lead with a two-amp fuse. The motor draws more at startup than I expected.

Section 1: Things to check before we power the radio
1. Inspect the electrolytic capacitors for bulging or leakage.
2. Look for solder bridges around the audio chip and the connector.
3. Check that the center pin of the power jack is positive.
4. Turn the supply current limit down before connecting the board.

I wrote these on a card and taped it to the shelf above the bench. I know we checked the polarity last time, but I want to verify it again because the jack footprint is not clearly marked on the board.
5. Keep the speaker disconnected until we have checked the output for a DC offset.

I found the radio in the cardboard box with the shortwave parts, and the cracked plastic case is worse than I remembered. One mounting post has broken away, and, I should say, the other three are intact. The tuning knob turns freely and the dial cord is still on its pulley, but the cord feels dry. I do not plan to replace it unless it slips. The board has a label that says “rev b” in blue marker, and a second label inside the case says “assembled in october twenty nineteen.” I could not find a schematic in the box. There is a handwritten note from Lewis that says, “The hiss got quieter when I moved the yellow wire,” but it does not say which yellow wire or what he changed. I took a photo before moving anything.

The main reason I want your help is to identify the audio input and the ground point without lifting parts from the board. I can trace the jack contacts with the meter in continuity mode, but the board has a large ground plane and several readings beep through nearby components. I have a small magnifier lamp now—well, technically, it is a clamp lamp with a magnifier lens—and it makes the silkscreen easier to read. The pad beside C14 may be ground, but I am not sure. The marking is partly hidden by old flux. If you can bring the board drawing from your folder, we can compare the connector names before testing anything. I have not connected the radio to the bench supply yet.

For the battery holder, I replaced the corroded spring contact with a salvaged contact from a toy, but I have not glued it in place. The holder takes four AA cells, and the spring is on the negative end. I cleaned the plastic with isopropyl alcohol and left it on the shelf overnight. The cells that came with the radio are too old to use, so I put them in the recycling tub. The battery leads are still attached to the board with their original red and black insulation. The black lead looks pinched where it passes through the case. I can add heat shrink after we decide whether the cable needs replacing. I have some twenty-six-gauge wire and red heat shrink in the small drawer.

I have laid out a few other items for Sunday so we do not have to stop halfway through the checks:
- A digital meter with fresh batteries.
- A small roll of solder that says “sixty thirty-seven tin lead.”
- A bottle of no-clean flux.
- The plastic spudger.
- My notebook with the measurements from the power supply test.

I also have the old headphones that crackle when the cable bends near the plug. They are not related to the radio, but the plug is the same size, and I would like to check whether the iron setup is comfortable for that repair too. I will bring a spare headphone cable in case the old one has broken inside the strain relief.

Please tell me if Sunday afternoon still works for you and whether you can bring the board drawing and your fine-tip tweezers.
